A content delivery network is a system of computers spread across many cities that store copies of websites and videos so they load faster. Normally, every request for a page travels back to one origin server, the original computer where the website's files live, no matter how far away the visitor happens to be. That trip takes time, especially over long distances, and if many people ask at once, the single computer can get overwhelmed. A content delivery network solves this by placing copies of the content on servers closer to visitors, called edge locations because they sit at the edge of the network, nearer everyday users rather than in one distant data center. When a visitor requests a page, the nearby edge location checks whether it already has a saved copy; finding one is called a cache hit, and it means the answer can be delivered instantly without contacting the origin at all. Think of it like a chain of neighborhood libraries holding copies of popular books, so nobody has to travel to the one central library across the country every time. Only when an edge location lacks the requested item does it fetch a fresh copy from the origin, then save it for next time. The result is quicker loading, less strain on the original server, and a smoother experience during busy periods.

| Term | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|------|----------------|-----------------|
| Origin server | The original computer storing a website's real files | Everything ultimately comes from here |
| Edge location | A nearby server holding copies of content | Shortens the distance data must travel |
| Cache hit | When a nearby copy is found and used | Delivers content instantly, skipping the origin |
| Content delivery network | The whole network of edge locations working together | Makes websites faster and more reliable overall |
